pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 9–10 years

- **Topic:** How energy travels around

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, England)):** HONEST NOTE: there is NO general 'energy' topic at KS2, so 'energy transfer' as such is not a primary statutory heading. The component phenomena are met in the primary topics — Sound (Y4: vibrations travel to the ear), Light (Y3/Y6), and especially Electricity (Y4: construct a simple series circuit; Y6: brightness vs number/voltage of cells) — and the electric-current transfer here sits directly on the Y4/Y6 Electricity content. But the unifying idea 'energy is transferred from place to place' is a KS3 idea in the UK. (Verified by fetch of gov.uk programmes of study.)

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** US National — NGSS 4-PS3-2 (this topic, essentially verbatim): '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-2].' Assessment boundary: 'does not include quantitative measurements of energy.' SEP Planning & Carrying Out Investigations (make observations to produce data as evidence); DCI PS3.A/PS3.B ('[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-2, 4-PS3-3]'; 'energy can be transferred… [curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-2, 4-PS3-4]'); CCC Energy and Matter. (Verified by fetch of nextgenscience.org 4-PS3-2.)

- **Operational details:** The child gathers EVIDENCE that energy moves from a SOURCE to a DESTINATION by four observable means — sound, light, heat and electric current. It stays qualitative and example-based: NO quantification of energy (the NGSS assessment boundary is explicit), and NOT yet the formal stores-and-pathways model (Tier B, mt_Jvg_r4yWaY). The conceptual seed being planted is direction and transfer: energy here → energy there, through a medium or pathway.

The child gives at least one example of each transfer — a buzzer/drum sends energy as sound to your ear; a lamp/Sun sends energy as light across a gap; a hot object warms a cooler one; a battery sends energy along wires to a bulb — and articulates that energy moves from where it starts to where it ends up. The most valuable framing (consistent with the later IOP model and with the NGSS DCI) is to treat sound, light, heat and electric current as the MEANS/pathway by which energy is shifted, not as 'stuff' in their own right: the bulb doesn't 'make' light-energy from nothing, it provides a pathway for energy from the battery to leave as light. Source → pathway → destination is the throughline.

Best taught by hands-on observation of each transfer (feel the warmth, hear the buzzer, trace the wire), explicitly identifying the source and the destination each time, and pressing for evidence ('how do you know energy got there?' — the bulb lit, the ear heard, the thermometer rose). The electric-current case leans on the prerequisite 'Building a simple circuit'.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A→B (observational, early bridge to formal, ≈9–10).
bestPractices: Give first-hand observation of each of the four transfers — feel the warmth from a hot object, hear the buzzer, trace the wire from battery to bulb, feel the Sun's light warm a surface — so the transfer is evidenced, not just asserted.
For every example name the SOURCE and the DESTINATION explicitly ('energy starts at the battery, ends at the bulb') — source→pathway→destination is the throughline that unifies all four cases.
Press for evidence that energy arrived: 'how do you know?' → the bulb lit, the ear heard, the thermometer rose — building the NGSS 'observations as evidence' practice.

Frame sound, light, heat and electric current as the MEANS by which energy is shifted, not as 'stuff' the device makes from nothing — the bulb provides a pathway for the battery's energy to leave as light (forward-compatible with the KS3 stores/pathways model).
Lean on the prerequisite circuit knowledge for the electric-current case: a complete loop lets energy reach the bulb; a break stops it.
Keep it strictly qualitative — no measuring or numbers for energy (respects the assessment boundary and the age).
keyRepresentations: Four paired source→destination scenes, one per transfer means (buzzer→ear, lamp/Sun→surface, hot object→cool object, battery→bulb)
A 'travelling energy' arrow/pulse running along each pathway from source to destination
A simple series circuit as the canonical electric-current transfer (battery → wires → bulb)
An evidence-of-arrival cue for each case (lit bulb, sounding ear, rising thermometer)
commonMisconceptions: Thinking a device 'makes' light/sound/heat from nothing rather than transferring energy that arrived from a source (the bulb 'contains' light) — misses source→destination.
Treating light, sound, heat and electric current as kinds of 'stuff' rather than means of transferring energy (the seed of the later store-vs-pathway error).
Believing energy is 'used up' on the way rather than transferred to the destination and surroundings.
Thinking electric current is 'used up' in the bulb (current consumed) rather than energy being delivered by the current as it passes — a common circuit companion error.
Assuming transfer needs touching in every case — not recognising light and radiated heat cross a gap (links to non-contact ideas in Forces).
Confusing the energy with the source object or the wire itself.

learn.summary: For ages 9\u201310: gather first-hand evidence that energy travels from a source to a destination by four observable means \u2014 sound, light, heat, and electric current. Throughout, name the source and destination explicitly, press for evidence that energy arrived (the bulb lit, the ear heard, the thermometer rose), and frame sound/light/heat/current as the MEANS by which energy is shifted rather than as 'stuff' a device makes from nothing. Stay strictly qualitative \u2014 no measuring or numbers for energy. The electric-current case depends on prior knowledge of a simple series circuit.

activities.title: Observe four transfers: source \u2192 pathway \u2192 destination
feedback: If a learner says 'the bulb makes the light': ask where the energy came from before the bulb lit \u2014 the bulb provides a pathway for energy from the battery to leave as light; it does not contain or create light from nothing.
If a learner asserts transfer without evidence: ask 'how do you know energy got there?' and steer them to the observable result (bulb lit, ear heard, thermometer/surface rose).

If a learner thinks transfer always needs touching: contrast the light/Sun case and radiated warmth crossing a gap with the hot-pan-to-spoon contact case \u2014 light and radiated heat cross a gap without touching.
If a learner says energy is 'used up on the way': reframe as energy transferred to the destination and its surroundings, not destroyed.

If a learner won't count sound or light as carrying energy ('they're just what you hear and see'): show light warming or illuminating a surface and a loud sound making something vibrate \u2014 they DO carry energy that can make something happen.

If a learner treats heat as a substance that 'leaks out' (the 'hotness' flows away): reframe heat as energy transferred from the hotter object to the cooler one because of the temperature difference \u2014 there is no 'heat stuff', just energy moving.
activities.rationale: First-hand observation of each transfer, with source and destination named and evidence of arrival demanded, builds the targeted 'make observations to provide evidence' practice and the unifying source\u2192pathway\u2192destination idea while respecting the qualitative, no-quantification boundary for this age.
sourceClaims: NGSS 4-PS3-2: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-2].' Assessment boundary: 'does not include quantitative measurements of energy.' DCI PS3.A/PS3.B: energy can be moved by moving objects, sound, light, electric currents; electric currents can [curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-2, 4-PS3-4].
learnerActions: Set up or observe each of four transfers and, for each, say out loud where the energy STARTS (source) and where it ENDS UP (destination): a buzzer/drum sends energy as sound to your ear; a lamp or the Sun sends energy as light across a gap to a surface; a hot object (e.g. a hot pan) warms a cooler one (e.g. a cold spoon) by contact; a battery sends energy along wires to a bulb.

For every case, answer 'How do you know the energy got there?' with the observed evidence \u2014 the bulb lit, the ear heard, the surface was lit up or warmed, the thermometer/spoon rose in temperature.
Before running each case, trace or draw an arrow from source to destination predicting the path the energy will take, then check it.
State for each case that energy moved from where it started to where it ended up, using the same 'source \u2192 pathway \u2192 destination' wording every time.
activities.intendedInsight: The same story \u2014 energy starts here, travels by some means, arrives there \u2014 holds across all four cases; energy is transferred from a source to a destination through a pathway, and you can evidence that it arrived.

activities.title: Make and break the electric pathway
feedback: If a learner thinks the current is 'used up' in the bulb: clarify that it is ENERGY that is transferred at the bulb, not the charge \u2014 the charge circulates round the loop and returns to the battery.
If a learner says the bulb stores or makes the light: point back to the break-the-loop observation \u2014 no complete path, no arrival, no light.

If the loop won't light, check for a break in the pathway (loose or wrong connections, a blown bulb) and also check the battery is not flat: the loop must be complete, and the battery must still have energy to give, for the bulb to light.
activities.rationale: Making and breaking the loop and observing arrival-or-not turns 'energy transfers' into something observed and sets up the distinction between charge circulating and energy being delivered. Treating current as a MEANS of transfer (not as 'stuff') is forward-compatible with the later stores-and-pathways model.
sourceClaims: England has no general 'energy' topic at KS2; the electric-current transfer sits on Y4 Electricity (construct a simple series circuit; whether a lamp lights in a complete loop) and Y6 Electricity (brightness/volume vs number and voltage of cells); the unifying 'energy transferred from place to place' idea is introduced at KS3.

Treating sound, light and electric current as the MEANS/pathway by which energy is transferred (not as energy 'stuff' in themselves) aligns with the IOP stores-and-pathways approach and avoids the later store-vs-pathway misconception.
learnerActions: Join a battery to a bulb with wires to complete a loop and observe the bulb light; then break the loop and observe the bulb go out.
Say what the complete loop allows ('energy can reach the bulb') and what the break stops ('energy can't get there').

Describe the chain: the battery gives energy to the current, the current carries energy along the wires to the bulb, where it is transferred to light and heat (an old-style filament bulb gives off much more heat than light).
Optionally, trace the energy arrow from battery to bulb before completing the circuit, then run it to check.
activities.intendedInsight: A complete circuit provides a pathway for energy to travel from the battery to the bulb; the bulb shines only because energy reached it, not because it 'contains' light.

activities.title: Reference panels and consolidation check
feedback: Matching or sorting errors: return to the lived observation \u2014 what did you see/hear/feel arrive, and from where?
If a learner categorises by the device rather than the means: separate the object (buzzer, lamp, pan, battery) from the means of transfer (sound, light, heat, current).

Note for teachers: these recognition tasks check classification after the fact; they can consolidate and check understanding but do not themselves elicit the first-hand observation of the transfer, so pair them with the hands-on activities.
activities.rationale: Matching, sorting, and reference panels reinforce the shared vocabulary and let learners distinguish the four means; recognition alone does not elicit the independent observation that defines the stated objective, so they accompany rather than replace the hands-on activities.
learnerActions: Use a labelled reference scene for each of the four transfers (source, pathway arrow, destination) and reveal 'how do you know it got there?' \u2014 the bulb lit / the ear heard / the thermometer rose.
Match each everyday example to its transfer means (sound, light, heat, electric current) and sort mixed scenarios by which means is at work.
Identify the evidence of arrival for a given scenario, and put a scenario in order: source \u2192 pathway \u2192 destination.
Trace a two-step example: a solar panel makes a fan spin \u2014 say where the energy came from and how many transfer means it used (light from the Sun, then electric current to the motor).
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidates the four cases and the source/destination language, and distinguishes the transfer means from each other and from the source object.

constraints: Keep strictly qualitative: no measuring or numbers for energy (respects the NGSS assessment boundary and the age range).
Do not introduce the formal stores-and-pathways model here; plant only the seed that energy moves source \u2192 via a means \u2192 destination.
The electric-current activity assumes prior knowledge of building a simple series circuit; if that is not secure, teach the circuit first.
Reference/matching/sorting tasks consolidate and check recognition of the means; they do not elicit independent observation of a transfer and should accompany, not replace, hands-on work.
A static or tap-to-reveal reference panel states the idea and reinforces vocabulary; it is a scaffold paired with hands-on observation, not a substitute for observing a transfer occur.

Optional interactive features (a travelling 'pulse' along each pathway, drag-to-wire a circuit, make/break the loop, aim a beam, a rising thermometer cue, trace-the-arrow predict mode) are illustrative ways to make the mechanism concrete, not mandatory mechanisms; first-hand physical observation is an equally valid vehicle.
Frame sound, light, heat, and electric current as means of transfer, not as substances; avoid implying a device creates energy from nothing.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row rated a dynamic 2D interactive as 'ideal' and claimed advantages 'no static medium can' deliver, and rated 3D/conversation as 'poor'. These are catalog fit preferences, not established comparative-efficacy findings; they have been softened to scaffold-with-stated-limits framing. Hands-on physical observation (feeling warmth, hearing a buzzer, tracing a real wire) is equally valid and retained as a primary vehicle.

The two-tier assessment's ammeter predict-measure task (equal readings before/after the bulb; charge conserved, energy transferred) is a sound diagnostic but assumes a measurement that sits near the edge of the no-quantification boundary; it is an assessment field, left unchanged, and not used as a learner teaching action here.

Non-contact transfer (light, radiated heat crossing a gap) is noted as a common-misconception correction; the hot-pan-to-spoon example is presented as the contact case and light/Sun as the across-a-gap case to avoid implying all transfer needs touching.

Activity 3's recognition-limit principle (recognition consolidates but does not elicit independent observation) is an objective-based inference; no cited source directly validates it, so its sourceClaims is left empty rather than borrowing the NGSS content claim on topic grounds.

assess.poeTask: Put an ammeter in the circuit just before the bulb, then just after it. Ask the child to predict whether the reading after the bulb will be smaller (because the bulb 'used some up'), the same, or larger — AND why. The consumption-model child predicts a smaller reading after the bulb; the transfer child predicts equal readings (charge conserved, only energy transferred). Then measure both.
probeDeeper: If you put an ammeter on each side of the bulb, what will the two readings be — and what does that tell you about whether current is 'used up'?
Give me one thing energy DOES when it arrives: at the bulb, at your ear from a speaker, at your skin from the Sun.
Counterexample: a solar panel makes a fan spin. Trace where the energy came from and how it travelled — how many transfer means did it use?
The bulb still lights after hours — if electricity were used up inside it, how could that be?
assess.correctAnswer: Current (moving charge) flows all the way round the complete loop — the same charge returns to the battery, it isn't used up. What the battery does is give energy to that current; the current carries the energy to the bulb, where it's transferred to light and heat. So energy travels from the battery to the bulb via the electric current, while the charge circulates and comes back.

errorPatterns.pattern: The battery sends electricity out to the bulb where it's used up, so less (or nothing) comes back — the consumption model.
errorPatterns.nextMove: It's ENERGY that's transferred at the bulb, not the charge — an ammeter reads the same before and after the bulb; the charge goes round and back.
errorPatterns.distractor: The battery sends electricity to the bulb, where it gets used up making light.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the current or electricity is consumed at the bulb.

errorPatterns.pattern: Sound and light just travel or spread but don't actually carry ENERGY ('they're not energy, they're just what you hear and see').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show light warming a surface and a loud sound making something vibrate — they DO carry energy that can do something.
errorPatterns.distractor: Sound and light aren't energy — they don't carry any energy from place to place.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Won't count sound or light as ways energy is transferred.

errorPatterns.pattern: Heat is a substance that flows out, rather than energy transferred from hot to cold ('the hotness leaks out').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Heat is energy transferred from hotter to cooler; there's no 'heat substance' — track energy from the warm source to the cooler surroundings.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes heat as a stuff or fluid rather than energy moving because of a temperature difference.

responseLevels.gap: Says electricity is sent out and used up in the bulb; won't count sound/light as energy carriers; treats heat as a substance.
responseLevels.full: Explains charge circulates round the loop (not consumed) while energy is delivered and transferred at the bulb, and identifies sound, light, heat and current as means by which energy travels from source to destination.
responseLevels.partial: Knows energy moves from a source to a destination and gives examples, but still says current is consumed in the bulb, or is unsure that sound and light carry energy.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A battery lights a bulb through wires. Does the battery send electricity OUT to the bulb where it gets used up, or does something travel round the whole loop? Explain what actually travels from the battery to the bulb, and what happens to it.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child with the 'current consumed in the bulb' model says electricity is sent out and used up; the transfer child distinguishes charge circulating (not consumed) from energy delivered and transferred at the bulb. The reason tier separates 'electricity gets used up in the bulb' from 'charge circulates, energy is delivered'.
